paragraphs.context: The Mole had been working very hard all the morning
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole is tired of cleaning his home. He throws down his brush, runs out, digs up through a tunnel and comes out in a sunny meadow.
paragraphs.simple: The Mole had worked very hard all morning. He was cleaning his little home for spring. First he used brooms, then dusters. Then he stood on ladders, steps and chairs, and used a brush and a bucket of whitewash. At last he had dust in his throat and eyes, white splashes all over his black fur, an aching back and tired arms. Spring was moving in the air above him and in the earth below and around him. It came even into his dark, low little house, and brought its special feeling of not being happy with what he had, and of wanting more. So it was not strange that he suddenly threw his brush down on the floor. He said, 'Bother!' and 'O blow!' and 'Hang spring-cleaning!' He ran out of the house without waiting to put on his coat. Something above was calling him in a strong way, as if it must be obeyed. He went to the steep little tunnel. For him it was the same as the gravel road in front of the house for animals whose homes are nearer the sun and air. He scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged, and then did it all again in another order. He worked busily with his little paws and said to himself, 'Up we go! Up we go!' At last, pop! his nose came out into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

paragraphs.context: He thought his happiness was complete when
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole sees a river for the first time. It looks to him like a living animal that tells stories.
paragraphs.simple: The Mole thought he could not be happier. Then, as he walked slowly along with no plan, he suddenly stood at the edge of a river that was full to the top. He had never seen a river before in his life. To him it was a smooth, curving, full-bodied animal. It chased and chuckled. It took hold of things with a gurgle and let them go with a laugh, and then it threw itself at new playmates. These shook themselves free, and were caught and held again. Everything was shaking and shivering. There were flashes and gleams and sparkles, rustle and swirl, chatter and bubble. The Mole was under a spell, full of wonder, and he could not stop looking. He trotted beside the river, like a small child who trots beside a man telling exciting stories. When he was tired at last, he sat on the bank. The river still chattered to him. It was a bubbling line of the best stories in the world, sent from the heart of the earth to be told at last to the sea that can never have enough.

paragraphs.context: whether you arrive at your destination or whether you reach somewhere else
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat says that it does not matter where a boat goes. He says that this is the charm of messing about in boats. He asks the Mole to go down the river with him.
paragraphs.simple: 'About in boats, or with boats,' the Rat went on calmly. He picked himself up and laughed in a pleasant way. 'In boats or out of them, it does not matter. Nothing seems really to matter, and that is the charm of it. You may get away, or you may not. You may arrive where you meant to go, or you may reach another place, or you may never get anywhere at all. You are always busy, and you never do anything in particular. When you have done it, there is always something else to do. You can do it if you like, but you had much better not. Look here! If you really have nothing else to do this morning, let us go down the river together and have a long day of it.'

paragraphs.context: The Rat was sitting on the river bank, singing a little song
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat has made up a song and does not listen to the Mole. He has been playing with the ducks, who were angry and sent him away.
paragraphs.simple: The Rat was sitting on the river bank and singing a little song. He had just made it up himself, so he was very full of it. He would not give proper attention to the Mole or to anything else. Since early morning he had been swimming in the river with his friends the ducks. When the ducks suddenly stood on their heads, as ducks do, he would dive down and tickle their necks, just under where their chins would be if ducks had chins. He did this until they had to come up again quickly, spluttering and angry and shaking their feathers at him. This is because you cannot say everything you feel when your head is under water. At last they begged him to go away, to look after his own business, and to leave them to look after theirs. So the Rat went away and sat on the river bank in the sun. He made up a song about them, which he called:

paragraphs.context: O, pooh! boating!” interrupted the Toad, in great disgust
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad says boating is a silly waste of time. He says he has found the only real way to spend a life, and he wants Rat and Mole to see it.
paragraphs.simple: 'Oh, pooh! Boating!' Toad said, in great disgust, as he cut in. 'It is a silly game for boys. I gave it up long ago. It is only a waste of time. It makes me really sorry to see you two, who should know better, use all your strength in that useless way. No, I have found the real thing, the only true work for a whole life. I plan to give the rest of my life to it. I can only be sorry for the wasted years behind me, which I threw away on little things. Come with me, dear Ratty, and your friendly friend too, if he will be so good. Come just as far as the stable-yard, and you will see what you will see!'

paragraphs.context: When they were quite ready, the now triumphant Toad led his companions
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad makes Rat and Mole catch the old grey horse, which does not want to go. Then they all start out on a golden afternoon.
paragraphs.simple: When they were quite ready, Toad was very proud of himself. He led his friends to the paddock and made them catch the old grey horse. Toad had chosen the horse for the dustiest job of this dusty trip, and had not asked him first. The horse was very angry about it. He liked the paddock better, and he took a lot of catching. Meanwhile Toad packed the lockers even tighter with things they needed. He hung nosebags, nets of onions, bundles of hay and baskets from the bottom of the cart. At last the horse was caught and harnessed, and they set off. They all talked at once. Each animal either walked beside the cart or sat on the shaft, as he felt like. It was a golden afternoon. The smell of the dust they kicked up was rich and pleasant. Birds called and whistled to them happily from thick orchards on both sides of the road. Friendly travellers who passed them said 'Good day', or stopped to say nice things about their beautiful cart. Rabbits sat at their front doors in the hedges, held up their front paws and said, 'O my! O my! O my!'

paragraphs.context: It was a cold, still afternoon with a hard, steely sky overhead
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole walks into the winter country. It is bare, and he likes its plain look. He goes on towards the Wild Wood.
paragraphs.simple: It was a cold, quiet afternoon. The sky above was hard and grey like steel. The Mole slipped out of the warm parlour into the open air. The land around him was bare, with no leaves at all. He thought he had never seen so far, and so closely, into the inside of things as on that winter day. Nature was deep in her yearly sleep, and seemed to have kicked the clothes off. The small woods, valleys, quarries and all hidden places had been secret mines to explore in leafy summer. Now they showed themselves and their secrets in a sad way. They seemed to ask him to forgive their poor, shabby look for a while, until they could play wild in rich dress again as before, and trick him and pull him in with the old tricks. In a way it was sad, and yet it was cheering, even exciting. He was glad that he liked the country plain and hard, with its fine dress taken away. He had come down to its bare bones, and they were fine and strong and simple. He did not want the warm clover or the seeding grasses. The thick hedges and the waving cover of beech and elm trees seemed better away. With great happiness he went on towards the Wild Wood. It lay in front of him, low and threatening, like a black reef in a quiet southern sea.

paragraphs.context: The pattering increased till it sounded like sudden hail
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole runs in panic and hides in a hollow tree. There he knows the Terror of the Wild Wood.
paragraphs.simple: The pattering grew until it sounded like sudden hail on the dry leaves spread around him. The whole wood seemed to be running now, running hard, hunting, chasing, closing in on something, or on someone. In a panic he began to run too, with no aim, and he did not know where. He ran into things, fell over things and into things, ran under things and went round things. At last he found shelter in the deep, dark hollow of an old beech tree. It gave shelter and hiding, and perhaps even safety, but who could tell? Anyway, he was too tired to run any further. He could only curl up in the dry leaves that had blown into the hollow, and hope he was safe for a time. He lay there panting and trembling, and listened to the whistling and the pattering outside. At last he knew it fully: the dreadful thing that other little animals of field and hedge had met here, and had known as their darkest moment. It was the thing that the Rat had tried in vain to keep him from. It was the Terror of the Wild Wood!

paragraphs.context: The Mole came and crouched beside him, and, looking out
paragraphs.mainIdea: The snow changes how the Wild Wood looks. The dark places are disappearing under a beautiful soft white cover.
paragraphs.simple: The Mole came and crouched beside the Rat. He looked out, and saw that the wood that had been so dreadful to him looked quite different. Holes, hollows, pools, hidden pits and other black dangers for the traveller were fast disappearing. A shining carpet like something from fairyland was growing everywhere. It looked too delicate for rough feet to walk on. A fine powder filled the air and touched the cheek with a tingle. The black trunks of the trees showed up in a light that seemed to come from below.

paragraphs.context: When at last they were thoroughly toasted, the Badger summoned them to the table
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Badger gives his guests a big supper. They are too hungry to talk, and he does not mind their bad manners.
paragraphs.simple: When they were warm all through, the Badger called them to the table, where he had been busy putting out a meal. They had felt quite hungry before. But when they saw the supper that was set out for them, the only question was what to eat first, where everything looked so good. They also wondered if the other things would be kind enough to wait until they had time for them. They could not talk for a long time. When they began to talk again, it was the sad kind of talk you get when you talk with your mouth full. The Badger did not mind this at all. He did not notice elbows on the table, or everybody talking at once. He did not go into Society himself, so he had an idea that these things did not really matter. (We know, of course, that he was wrong and saw it in too narrow a way, because they do matter very much. But it would take too long to say why.) He sat in his armchair at the head of the table. He nodded in a serious way now and then as the animals told their story. He did not seem surprised or shocked at anything. He never said, 'I told you so,' or 'Just what I always said,' or that they should have done this, or should not have done that. The Mole began to feel very friendly towards him.

paragraphs.context: His two friends assented, quite understanding his point
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat and the Mole understand that no animal is expected to do hard things in winter. In winter all animals are sleepy and resting.
paragraphs.simple: His two friends agreed. They understood what he meant. By the rules of animal etiquette, no animal is ever expected to do anything that takes great effort, or anything brave, or even anything fairly active, in the winter, when there is little to do. All of them are sleepy, and some are really asleep. All are kept indoors by the weather, more or less. All are resting after hard days and nights, when every muscle has been tested hard and all their strength has been used to the full.

paragraphs.context: It would be astonishing indeed,” said the Badger simply
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Badger says that he did not build the tunnels. He says that a city of people stood there long ago.
paragraphs.simple: 'It would be astonishing indeed,' said the Badger plainly, 'if I had done it. But in fact I did none of it. I only cleaned out the passages and rooms, as far as I needed them. There is a lot more of it, all round. I see you do not understand, and I must explain it to you. Well, very long ago, on the place where the Wild Wood waves now, before it had planted itself and grown to what it is now, there was a city. It was a city of people. Here, where we are standing, they lived and walked and talked and slept, and did their business. Here they kept their horses and had feasts. From here they rode out to fight, or drove out to trade. They were a strong, rich people, and great builders. They built to last, because they thought their city would last for ever.'

paragraphs.context: Poor Mole stood alone in the road, his heart torn asunder
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole wants to go to his old home, but he will not leave his friend. At last he follows the Rat down the road.
paragraphs.simple: Poor Mole stood alone in the road. His heart was torn in two, and a big sob was growing low inside him. He knew it would soon jump up in a wild rush. But even now he stayed loyal to his friend. He never thought for a moment of leaving him. Meanwhile the smells from his old home begged and whispered and made a spell on him. At last they called him in a way he had to obey. He did not dare to stay longer in their magic circle. With a hard pull on his deepest feelings, he turned his face down the road and followed the Rat's track without arguing. Faint, thin little smells still followed his nose as it moved away. They blamed him for his new friendship and for forgetting his home in such a hard way.

paragraphs.context: The Mole subsided forlornly on a tree stump and tried to control himself
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole sits on a stump and cries because he cannot go to his old home.
paragraphs.simple: The Mole sat down sadly on a tree stump and tried to control himself, because he felt that the sob was surely coming. He had fought it for so long, but it would not be beaten. It forced its way up into the air. Then came another, and another, and others very fast. At last poor Mole gave up the fight. He cried freely and helplessly and in the open, now that he knew it was all over. He had lost something that he could hardly be said to have found.

paragraphs.context: He clambered into his bunk and rolled himself well up in the blankets
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat climbs into his bunk and falls asleep at once.
paragraphs.simple: He climbed into his bunk and rolled himself well up in the blankets. Sleep took him at once, as a long line of cut corn is taken up by the machine that cuts it.

paragraphs.context: another new and exceptionally powerful motorcar will arrive at Toad Hall
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Badger says that Toad will soon have another new motorcar. He says that the three of them must go to Toad Hall now and rescue Toad.
paragraphs.simple: 'This very morning,' the Badger went on, as he took an armchair, 'another new and very powerful motorcar will arrive at Toad Hall. I learnt this last night from a source I can trust. Toad can keep it, or send it back if he does not like it. Perhaps at this very moment Toad is busy dressing himself in those very ugly clothes that he loves. They change him from a Toad who is fairly good-looking into a thing that makes any decent animal very angry when it sees it. We must get up and do something before it is too late. You two animals will come with me to Toad Hall at once, and we shall do the work of rescue.'

paragraphs.context: They had to lay Toad out on the floor, kicking
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat and the Mole take off Toad's motor clothes. Without them, Toad is no longer a proud driver.
paragraphs.simple: They had to lay Toad out on the floor, while he kicked and called them all sorts of names. Only then could they begin their work. The Rat sat on him, and the Mole took his motor clothes off him bit by bit. They stood him on his legs again. Much of his loud, proud spirit seemed to have gone when his fine clothes were taken away. Now he was only Toad, and no longer the Terror of the Highway. He gave a weak giggle and looked at them one after the other, as if asking for kindness. He seemed to understand the situation well.

paragraphs.context: the brutal minions of the law fell upon the hapless Toad
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad is judged and taken through a crowd and a castle to a dungeon. At the end they stop at a dungeon door, where an old gaoler sits.
paragraphs.simple: Then the cruel servants of the law fell on poor Toad. They put chains on him and dragged him from the Court House, while he screamed, begged and protested. They took him across the marketplace. There the crowd were hard on a crime that had been found, but kind to a man who was only 'wanted'. They shouted mocking words at him, threw carrots and shouted popular sayings. They went past school children who hooted. Their innocent faces were lit up with the pleasure they always get from the sight of a gentleman in trouble. Then they crossed the hollow-sounding drawbridge, went under the spiky gate that is let down, and passed under the dark archway of the grim old castle, whose ancient towers rose high above. They went past guardrooms full of grinning soldiers who were off duty. They went past guards who coughed in a nasty, mocking way, because that is as much as a guard on duty dares to do to show how he hates crime. They went up old, worn, winding stairs, past men in steel armour who gave him threatening looks through their face guards. They crossed courtyards where big dogs pulled on their leads and pawed the air to get at him. They went past old guards, who had leant their long axes on poles against the wall and were dozing over a pie and a large jug of brown ale. On and on they went, past the rack-room and the thumbscrew-room, and past the turning that led to the private place of execution. At last they came to the door of the grimmest dungeon, in the middle of the innermost tower. There they stopped, where an old gaoler sat, playing with a bunch of great keys.

paragraphs.context: The Willow-Wren was twittering his thin little song
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is a hot summer night. The Mole lies on the bank and waits for the Rat, who is out late with Otter.
paragraphs.simple: The Willow-Wren was singing his thin little song, hidden in the dark edge of the river bank. It was past ten o'clock at night, but the sky still held some last light from the day that had gone. The heavy heat of the very hot afternoon broke up and rolled away at the cool touch of the short midsummer night. The Mole lay stretched on the bank, still breathing hard after the fierce day. It had been cloudless from dawn to late sunset. He waited for his friend to come back. He had been on the river with some friends, and the Water Rat had been free to keep an old plan with Otter. When he came home, he found the house dark and empty, and no sign of Rat, who was probably staying out late with his old friend. It was still too hot to think of staying indoors. So he lay on some cool dock leaves, and thought over the day and what had happened in it, and how very good it all had been.

paragraphs.context: Well, it seems that it was there he gave Portly his first swimming-lesson
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat explains why Otter watches by the ford. It is where he taught Portly to swim and to fish.
paragraphs.simple: 'Well, it seems that he gave Portly his first swimming lesson there,' the Rat went on. 'It was from that shallow, stony spit of land near the bank. He also used to teach him to fish there, and there young Portly caught his first fish. He was very proud of it. The child loved the place. Otter thinks that Portly may come wandering back from wherever he is, if he is anywhere by now, poor little chap. He might make for the ford that he was so fond of. Or if he came across it, he would remember it well and stop there and play, perhaps. So Otter goes there every night and watches, on the chance, you know, just on the chance!'

paragraphs.context: Perhaps he would never have dared to raise his eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole is afraid, but he must look. He sees the Friend and Helper with the baby otter asleep between his hooves.
paragraphs.simple: Perhaps he would never have dared to raise his eyes. But the piping had stopped, and the call and the summons still seemed strong and had to be obeyed. He could not say no, even if Death himself were waiting to strike him at once, after he had looked with human eyes on things that should stay hidden. He obeyed, trembling, and raised his humble head. Then, in the clear light of the dawn that was about to come, while Nature was filled with colours too bright to be believed and seemed to hold her breath for what would happen, he looked into the very eyes of the Friend and Helper. He saw the curved horns sweeping back, shining in the growing daylight. He saw the stern, hooked nose between the kind eyes, which were looking down on them with amusement. The bearded mouth was breaking into a half-smile at the corners. He saw the moving muscles on the arm that lay across the broad chest. He saw the long, strong hand that still held the pan-pipes, which had only just fallen away from the open lips. He saw the fine curves of the rough, hairy legs, resting in grand ease on the grass. Last of all he saw the little, round, fat, childish shape of the baby otter. It was sleeping soundly in perfect peace between his very hooves. He saw all this for one moment, breathless and strong, bright against the morning sky. And still, as he looked, he lived; and still, as he lived, he wondered.

paragraphs.context: As they stared blankly, in dumb misery deepening as they slowly realised
paragraphs.mainIdea: A breeze makes the two animals forget what they saw. This gift of forgetting keeps the memory from spoiling their lives.
paragraphs.simple: They stared with no thought in their eyes. They were silent and sad, and the sadness grew as they slowly understood all they had seen and all they had lost. Then a little breeze that changed its way for no reason came dancing up from the water. It shook the aspen trees and the roses with dew on them, and blew gently on their faces. With its soft touch came sudden forgetting. This is the last and best gift that the kind demigod is careful to give to those he has shown himself to when he helped them. It is the gift of forgetting. It is given so that the awful memory should not stay and grow and cast a shadow on their happiness and fun. It is given so that the great memory that would not leave them should not spoil all the later lives of little animals who have been helped out of trouble. In this way they can be happy and light-hearted as before.

paragraphs.context: When Toad found himself immured in a dank and noisome dungeon
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad is in the dungeon and is very sad. He thinks it is the end of everything, and he is sorry for himself.
paragraphs.simple: Toad found himself shut in a cold, wet dungeon with a bad smell. He knew that all the dark of an old castle lay between him and the outside world. In that world there was sunshine, and there were good high roads, where he had lately been so happy, playing as if he had bought every road in England. He threw himself down on the floor at full length, and cried bitter tears, and gave himself up to dark despair. 'This is the end of everything,' he said, 'or at least it is the end of the career of Toad, which is the same thing. The popular and handsome Toad, the rich and kind-to-guests Toad, the Toad so free and careless and gay! How can I hope ever to be free again,' he said, 'when I have been put in prison so fairly? I stole such a handsome motorcar in such a bold way, and I gave such wild and clever cheek to so many fat, red-faced policemen!' (Here his crying stopped his words.) 'What a stupid animal I was,' he said. 'Now I must sit in this dungeon until the people who were proud to say they knew me have forgotten the very name of Toad! O wise old Badger!' he said, 'O clever, intelligent Rat and sensible Mole! What sound judgments, what knowledge of men and things you have! O unhappy and left-alone Toad!' He spent his days and nights like this for several weeks. He would not eat his meals or the light snacks between them. But the old gaoler knew that Toad's pockets were full, and he often said that many comforts, and even luxuries, could be sent in from outside, for a price.

paragraphs.context: The smell of that buttered toast simply talked to Toad
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gaoler's daughter brings tea and buttered toast. The smell reminds Toad of his home, and he begins to talk about himself.
paragraphs.simple: When the girl came back some hours later, she carried a tray. On it was a cup of sweet-smelling tea, with steam rising from it, and a plate piled high with very hot buttered toast. It was cut thick and very brown on both sides, and the butter ran through the holes in it in great golden drops, like honey from the honeycomb. The smell of that buttered toast simply talked to Toad, in a voice that he could clearly understand. It talked of warm kitchens, of breakfasts on bright frosty mornings, and of cosy firesides in the parlour on winter evenings, when your walk was over and your feet in slippers were up on the fender. It talked of the purring of happy cats, and the twitter of sleepy canaries. Toad sat up again, dried his eyes, sipped his tea and chewed his toast. Soon he began to talk freely about himself, and the house he lived in, and what he did there, and how important he was, and what a lot his friends thought of him.

paragraphs.context: In his misery he made one desperate effort to carry the thing off
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad has no money for a ticket. He tries to carry it off by acting like a fine gentleman who has left his purse behind.
paragraphs.simple: In his misery Toad made one desperate try to carry it off. He went back to his fine old manner, a mix of the Squire and the College Don. He said, 'Look here! I find I have left my purse behind. Just give me that ticket, will you, and I will send the money on tomorrow? I am well known in these parts.'

paragraphs.context: As he walked along, considering, his attention was caught by some red
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad sees the lights of a railway station and thinks it is a piece of luck. He does not want to go through the town.
paragraphs.simple: As he walked along, thinking, he saw some red and green lights a little way off, at one side of the town. He heard the puffing and snorting of engines and the banging of trucks that were being moved. 'Aha!' he thought. 'This is a piece of luck! A railway station is the thing I want most in the whole world at this moment. And what is more, I need not go through the town to get it. I shall not have to keep up this shameful part by quick answers. They are very good, but they do not help one's feeling of self-respect.'

paragraphs.context: Nature’s Grand Hotel has its Season, like the others
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book compares the year to a grand hotel. In autumn the guests leave one by one, and those who stay feel unsettled.
paragraphs.simple: The Grand Hotel of Nature has its Season, like all the others. The guests pack, pay and leave one by one. At each meal there are fewer seats at the shared table. Suites of rooms are closed, carpets are taken up, and waiters are sent away. Those guests who are staying on until the hotel opens fully next year cannot help being a little affected by all these comings and goings. They hear the eager talk of plans, routes and new places, and they see the stream of friends become smaller each day. One gets unsettled, sad and likely to complain. Why this wish for change? Why not stay on quietly here, like us, and be happy? You do not know this hotel out of the season, or what fun we have among ourselves, we who stay and see the whole interesting year out. 'All very true, no doubt,' the others always answer. 'We quite envy you. Some other year, perhaps. But just now we have things to do, and the bus is at the door. Our time is up!' So they leave, with a smile and a nod, and we miss them and feel angry. The Rat was an animal who needed nothing from others, and was fixed to the land. Whoever went, he stayed. Still, he could not help seeing what was in the air, and feeling some of its power in his bones.

paragraphs.context: I tried ‘stopping on’ one year,” said the third swallow
paragraphs.mainIdea: The third swallow says that it once stayed behind and had a bad winter. It then flew south and was happy, and it has always obeyed the call since.
paragraphs.simple: 'I tried "stopping on" one year,' said the third swallow. 'I had grown so fond of the place that when the time came I hung back and let the others go on without me. For a few weeks it was all well enough. But afterwards, oh, the weary length of the nights! The shivering days with no sun! The air so cold and wet, and not an insect in a whole acre of it! No, it was no good. My courage broke down, and one cold, stormy night I took wing. I flew well inland, because of the strong east winds. It was snowing hard as I beat my way through the passes of the great mountains, and I had a hard fight to get through. But I shall never forget the happy feeling of the hot sun on my back again as I flew down to the lakes that lay so blue and calm below me, and the taste of my first fat insect! The past was like a bad dream. The future was all happy holiday as I moved south week by week, easily and lazily, staying as long as I dared, but always listening to the call. No, I had had my warning. Never again did I think of disobeying.'

paragraphs.context: The wayfarer was lean and keen-featured, and somewhat bowed at the shoulders
paragraphs.mainIdea: The new rat who comes along the road is thin and sharp-faced. He wears small gold earrings and blue clothes.
paragraphs.simple: The traveller was thin, with a sharp face, and his shoulders were a little bent. His paws were thin and long, and his eyes had many lines at the corners. He wore small gold earrings in his neat, well-shaped ears. His knitted jersey was a faded blue. His trousers were mended and stained, but they were blue underneath. The small things that he carried were tied up in a blue cotton handkerchief.

paragraphs.context: He had the world all to himself, that early summer morning
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad walks alone in the morning and looks for a road that can tell him the way. He is looking for something that can talk and tell him which way to go.
paragraphs.simple: He had the world all to himself that early summer morning. The woodland was wet with dew, and he walked through it, and it was lonely and quiet. The green fields after the trees were his own, to do with as he liked. When he reached the road, it seemed to be looking anxiously for company, like a stray dog, in the loneliness that was everywhere. But Toad was looking for something that could talk and tell him clearly which way to go. It is all very well to follow where the road calls and points, without caring where it goes. This is when you have a light heart, a clear conscience and money in your pocket, and nobody is searching the country to drag you off to prison again. But Toad was a practical animal and he cared very much. He could have kicked the road for its helpless silence, when every minute mattered to him.

paragraphs.context: A long half-hour passed, and every minute of it saw Toad getting crosser
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad tries to wash the clothes, but he cannot do it. He gets very angry and his paws start to get wrinkled.
paragraphs.simple: A long half-hour passed, and each minute of it saw Toad getting angrier. Nothing he did to the clothes seemed to please them or do them any good. He tried coaxing, he tried slapping, and he tried punching. They smiled back at him from the tub, not changed, and happy in their original sin. Once or twice he looked nervously over his shoulder at the barge-woman, but she seemed to be looking out in front of her and thinking only of her steering. His back ached badly, and he saw with dismay that his paws were starting to get crinkly. Now Toad was very proud of his paws. He said under his breath words that should never pass the lips of washerwomen or of Toads. And he lost the soap for the fiftieth time.

paragraphs.context: He had travelled some miles, his horse and he, and he was feeling drowsy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad finds a gipsy cooking a stew. The smell makes Toad very hungry. He wonders if he can fight the gipsy or charm him.
paragraphs.simple: He had travelled some miles, he and his horse, and he was feeling sleepy in the hot sun. Then the horse stopped, put his head down and began to bite the grass. Toad woke up, and only just kept himself from falling off. He looked round and found that he was on a wide common with patches of gorse and bramble as far as he could see. Near him stood a dull-looking gipsy caravan. Beside it a man was sitting on a bucket turned upside down. He was very busy smoking and looking out at the wide world. A fire of sticks was burning near by, and an iron pot hung over it. Out of the pot came bubbling and gurgling sounds, and a vague, hinting cloud of steam. There were also smells, warm, rich and of many kinds. They twisted together at last into one complete, perfect smell. It seemed like the very soul of Nature taking form and appearing to her children, a true Goddess, a mother of comfort. Toad now knew well that he had not really been hungry before. What he had felt earlier in the day was only a small sick feeling. This was the real thing at last, and no mistake. It would have to be dealt with fast, or somebody or something would be in trouble. He looked the gipsy over carefully, and wondered if it would be easier to fight him or to charm him. So he sat there, and sniffed and sniffed, and looked at the gipsy. And the gipsy sat and smoked, and looked at him.

paragraphs.context: Now, it was a very comforting point in Toad’s character
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad is good-hearted and does not mind when his friends speak to him sharply. He says he is sorry, but he also has a new idea about motorboats.
paragraphs.simple: Now, it was a very comforting point in Toad's character that he was a thoroughly good-hearted animal. He never minded being scolded by those who were his real friends. Even when he was most set on something, he was always able to see the other side of the question. While the Rat was talking so seriously, Toad kept saying to himself in a rebel way, 'But it was fun, though! Awful fun!' He made strange noises inside him that he held back: k-i-ck-ck-ck, and poop-p-p, and other sounds like hidden snorts or the opening of soda-water bottles. But when the Rat had quite finished, he gave a deep sigh and said, very nicely and humbly, 'Quite right, Ratty! How sound you always are! Yes, I have been a conceited old ass, I can see that. But now I am going to be a good Toad, and not do it any more. As for motorcars, I have not been at all so keen on them since my last ducking in that river of yours. The fact is, while I was hanging on to the edge of your hole and getting my breath, I had a sudden idea, a really clever idea, about motorboats. There, there! Do not get so upset, old chap, and stamp, and knock things over. It was only an idea, and we will not talk any more about it now. We will have our coffee, and a smoke, and a quiet chat. Then I am going to stroll quietly down to Toad Hall, and get into clothes of my own, and start things going again as before. I have had enough of adventures. I shall lead a quiet, steady, respectable life, doing little jobs about my property, and making it better, and doing a little landscape gardening at times. There will always be a bit of dinner for my friends when they come to see me. And I shall keep a pony-chaise to go about the country in, just as I used to in the good old days, before I got restless and wanted to do things.'

paragraphs.context: Well, it was a good deal talked about down here, naturally
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat says the animals took sides when Toad went to prison. The Wild Wood animals said hard things, and the River-bankers stood up for him.
paragraphs.simple: 'Well, it was talked about a lot down here, naturally,' the Rat went on. 'It was talked about not only along the river, but even in the Wild Wood. The animals took sides, as always happens. The River-bankers stood up for you. They said you had been treated in a shameful way, and that there was no justice to be had in the land nowadays. But the Wild Wood animals said hard things. They said it served you right, and that it was time this sort of thing was stopped. They got very sure of themselves, and went about saying that you were finished this time. They said you would never come back again, never, never!'

paragraphs.context: They argued from history,” continued the Rat. “They said that no criminal laws
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Mole and the Badger moved into Toad Hall. Then one dark night weasels, ferrets and stoats came in from all sides.
paragraphs.simple: 'They argued from the past,' the Rat went on. 'They said that no criminal laws had ever been known to win against cheek and good talk like yours, with the power of a full purse. So they arranged to move their things into Toad Hall, and sleep there, and keep it aired, and have it all ready for you when you came back. They did not guess what was going to happen, of course. But they did have their doubts about the Wild Wood animals. Now I come to the most painful and sad part of my story. One dark night (it was a very dark night, with a hard wind and the rain coming down in buckets) a band of weasels, with weapons of every kind, crept up the carriage-drive to the front door. At the same moment a group of fierce ferrets came through the kitchen-garden and took the backyard and the other rooms. A company of stoats, who would stop at nothing, took the conservatory and the billiard-room. They also held the French windows that opened on to the lawn.'

paragraphs.context: The Mole and the Badger were sitting by the fire in the smoking-room
paragraphs.mainIdea: The weasels and stoats attack the Mole and the Badger and throw them out into the cold and wet.
paragraphs.simple: 'The Mole and the Badger were sitting by the fire in the smoking-room, telling stories and suspecting nothing, because it was not a night for any animals to be out in. Then those wicked villains broke down the doors and rushed in on them from every side. They fought as well as they could, but what was the good? They had no weapons and were taken by surprise, and what can two animals do against hundreds? The weasels and stoats took them and beat them hard with sticks, those two poor faithful creatures. They turned them out into the cold and the wet, and said many insulting and unfair things.'

paragraphs.context: It was cold, and dark, and damp, and low, and narrow
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the dark passage Toad is afraid and falls behind. When he rushes forward, he knocks the others over, and the Badger nearly shoots him.
paragraphs.simple: It was cold, and dark, and damp, and low, and narrow, and poor Toad began to shiver. He shivered partly from fear of what might be before him, and partly because he was wet through. The lantern was far ahead, and he could not help staying behind a little in the darkness. Then he heard the Rat call out as a warning, 'Come on, Toad!' A terror took hold of him of being left behind, alone in the darkness, and he 'came on' with such a rush that he knocked the Rat into the Mole, and the Mole into the Badger, and for a moment all was confusion. The Badger thought they were being attacked from behind. There was no room to use a stick or a cutlass, so he drew a pistol, and he was about to put a bullet into Toad. When he found out what had really happened he was very angry indeed, and said, 'Now this time that tiresome Toad shall be left behind!'

paragraphs.context: Sometimes, in the course of long summer evenings, the friends would take a stroll
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the end the friends walk in the Wild Wood, where the animals now greet them with respect. The mother-weasels talk about them to their babies.
paragraphs.simple: Sometimes, on long summer evenings, the friends would take a walk together in the Wild Wood, which was now made safe, as far as they were concerned. It was pleasing to see how respectfully the animals who lived there greeted them. The mother-weasels would bring their young ones to the mouths of their holes and say, pointing, 'Look, baby! There goes the great Mr. Toad! And that is the brave Water Rat, a terrible fighter, walking along with him! And over there comes the famous Mr. Mole, of whom you have so often heard your father tell!' But when their babies were cross and quite beyond control, they would quiet them by telling how the terrible grey Badger would get them if they did not hush them and not fret them. This was a mean and false thing to say about the Badger. He cared little about Society, but he was rather fond of children. Still, it never failed to work.

paragraphs.context: All along the backwater, Through the rushes tall, Ducks are
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the Rat's song about ducks who put their heads down in the river and their tails up.
paragraphs.simple: The song is called Ducks' Ditty. Along the quiet side water, through the tall water plants, the ducks splash with their tails up. Ducks and the male ducks have yellow feet that shake and yellow beaks busy in the river. Under the green plants, where the river fish swim, they keep their food store, cool and full and dim. Everyone may like what they like. The ducks like to be heads down and tails up, splashing freely. High in the blue sky, fast birds fly and call. The ducks stay down in the water, tails up.

paragraphs.context: Villagers all, this frosty tide, Let your doors swing open wide
paragraphs.mainIdea: The field-mice sing an old Christmas song at Mole's door, asking to come in out of the cold.
paragraphs.simple: The mice sing a Christmas song. They ask the people of the village to open their doors on this cold night, even if wind and snow come too, and to let the singers sit by the fire. They promise joy in the morning. They are standing in the cold, blowing on their fingers and stamping their feet. They have come from far away to greet the people who are warm inside, while the singers are still in the street. A star led them in the night. They sing of Joseph working through the snow, of a low stable, and of Mary, who could go no farther. They sing that animals were the first to hear the angels and to cry out the good news. Joy will be theirs in the morning.

paragraphs.context: Lest the awe should dwell And turn your frolic to fret
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rat repeats a strange song from the reeds. It says the hearer will forget this power.
paragraphs.simple: The Rat, with his eyes still shut, tries to give Mole the words of the music. They are faint but clear. The song says: do not let the wonder stay and turn your play into worry. You may look on this power at the hour when you need help, but then you will forget. The reeds take up the song and sigh forget, forget, until it dies away. Then the voice starts to come back.

paragraphs.context: the Vision had vanished, and the air was full of the carol
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wonderful figure is gone. Ordinary sunrise and bird-song take its place.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the sun's wide gold circle comes up over the line of the sky in front of them. The first light shoots across the flat wet meadows and shines straight into the animals' eyes, so they cannot see. When they can look again, the great figure has gone. The air is full of birds singing to the morning.

paragraphs.context: The world has held great Heroes, As history-books have showed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad sings a boastful song that says he is greater than heroes, scholars, and kings.
paragraphs.simple: Toad sings that the world has had great heroes, as history books show, but no famous name can compare with Toad. He says the clever men at Oxford know all that can be known, but he uses a made-up word, knowed, so the line will rhyme. He says none of them know half as much as he does. He says the animals in the boat cried, and he was the one who said there was land ahead. He says the army saluted as they marched, and it was not the king, it was Mr. Toad. He says the queen and her ladies sat sewing at the window, and when she asked who that handsome man was, they answered Mr. Toad.

paragraphs.context: The motorcar went Poop-poop-poop, As it raced along the road
paragraphs.mainIdea: Toad starts another boastful song, about steering a motorcar into a pond.
paragraphs.simple: Toad sings that the motorcar made its horn noise as it raced along the road, and that he was the clever one who steered it into a pond. The song is only a few lines. He is too full of himself to finish it properly.

paragraphs.context: There was panic in the parlours and howling in the halls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alone in his room, Toad sings a loud song about coming home as a hero.
paragraphs.simple: Toad sings his last little song to the empty chairs. He sings that when he came home there was panic in the sitting rooms and howling in the halls, crying in the cow houses and shrieking in the stalls. Windows were smashed and doors crashed in, and weasels were chased until they fainted. Drums bang. Trumpet players toot, soldiers salute, cannon shoot, and motorcars hoot as the hero comes. He tells the crowd to shout hooray very loud, in honour of an animal they are proud of, because it is Toad's great day.

paragraphs.context: a faint Poop-poop wailed like an uneasy animal in pain
paragraphs.mainIdea: The coming motorcar is pictured as a living thing: first a bee, then an animal in pain, then a bee again.
paragraphs.simple: Mole, Rat, and Toad are walking easily along the high road. Mole talks to the horse, who feels left out. Toad talks, and Rat only says yes and thinks of something else. Far behind them they hear a faint warning hum, like a bee far away. They look back and see a small cloud of dust with a dark centre, coming at a huge speed. Out of the dust a faint horn-cry wails like a hurt animal. They hardly look, and turn back to their talk. Then, in an instant, the quiet scene changes. Wind and noise make them jump for the nearest ditch. The thing is on them. The horn rings like a shout. For a moment they see shining glass and rich leather, and a huge motorcar, with its driver tense and holding the wheel. It owns earth and air for a second, throws a cloud of dust over them so they cannot see, and then shrinks to a speck far away, a droning bee once more.

sentences.context: penetrating even his dark and lowly little house with its spirit
sentences.simple: Spring came even into his dark, low little house and brought a special feeling of not being happy with what he had, and of wanting more.
sentences.grammar: 'penetrating ...' is a participle phrase that tells what spring was doing while it moved; 'with its spirit of ...' says what spring brought.

sentences.context: Never in his life had he seen a river before
sentences.simple: In all his life he had not seen a river before. This smooth, curving, full-bodied animal chased and chuckled. It took hold of things with a gurgle and let them go with a laugh, and threw itself at new playmates, which shook themselves free and were caught and held again.
sentences.grammar: Inversion: after 'Never in his life' at the start, 'had' comes before 'he' ('had he seen'). The dash then adds a long description of the river.

sentences.context: whether you arrive at your destination or whether you reach somewhere else
sentences.simple: Whether you get away or you do not, whether you arrive where you meant to go or reach some other place, or never get anywhere at all, you are always busy and you never do anything in particular. When you have done it there is always something else to do. You can do it if you like, but you had much better not.
sentences.grammar: 'whether ... or whether ...' gives two choices and says the result is the same for both; 'whether' is used four times, and the main clause 'you're always busy' comes after them.

sentences.context: What it hasn’t got is not worth having
sentences.simple: What the river does not have is not worth having, and what it does not know is not worth knowing.
sentences.grammar: 'What it hasn't got' is a noun clause that is the subject of the sentence; 'worth + -ing' means good enough to be done or had.

sentences.context: Since early morning he had been swimming in the river
sentences.simple: He had been swimming in the river with his friends the ducks since early in the morning.
sentences.grammar: 'had been swimming' is the past perfect continuous: the swimming began before that moment and went on up to it; 'since' gives the start time.

sentences.context: and it may be that he is both boastful and conceited
sentences.simple: And it may be that he both boasts and thinks too much of himself.
sentences.grammar: 'it may be that ...' means 'perhaps'; 'both ... and ...' joins two words that are true together.

sentences.context: I propose to devote the remainder of mine to it
sentences.simple: I plan to give the rest of my life to it. I can only be sorry for the wasted years behind me, which I threw away on little things.
sentences.grammar: 'propose to + verb' means 'plan to' in formal speech; 'mine' stands for 'my life', which was said just before; 'squandered in trivialities' is a past participle phrase about 'the wasted years'.

sentences.context: Disregarding the Rat, he proceeded to play upon the inexperienced Mole
sentences.simple: Toad did not listen to the Rat. He went on to play on the Mole, who had little experience, as if the Mole were a harp.
sentences.grammar: 'Disregarding the Rat' is a participle phrase that tells what Toad did while he went on; 'proceeded to + verb' means 'went on to'; 'as on a harp' is a comparison.

sentences.context: Hardly regarding it, they turned to resume their conversation
sentences.simple: They hardly looked at it. They turned to start their talk again, when in a moment (as it seemed) the peaceful scene was changed. There was a blast of wind and a whirl of sound that made them jump for the nearest ditch.
sentences.grammar: 'Hardly regarding it' is a participle phrase meaning 'paying it almost no attention'; 'when in an instant ...' adds the sudden change.

sentences.context: he had never seen so far and so intimately into the insides of things
sentences.simple: He thought he had never seen so far, and so closely, into the inside of things as on that winter day, when Nature was deep in her yearly sleep and seemed to have kicked the clothes off.
sentences.grammar: 'had never seen' is the past perfect inside what he thought; 'so far and so intimately' joins two adverbs, and 'as on that winter day' compares.

sentences.context: and as if it had been so all the time, every hole
sentences.simple: Then suddenly, as if it had been like this all the time, every hole, near and far, seemed to have its face. There were hundreds of them. All the faces came and went fast, and every one looked at him with hate and a wish to hurt him, hard-eyed and evil and sharp.
sentences.grammar: 'as if it had been so' uses the past perfect after 'as if' to say how things seemed; the words 'and there were hundreds of them' are a side remark between commas.

sentences.context: it broke out on either side, and seemed to be caught up
sentences.simple: As he stopped, not able to decide, the whistle came from both sides. It seemed that others took it up and passed it on along the whole wood, to its farthest end.
sentences.grammar: 'seemed to be caught up and passed on' is 'seemed to be' plus two past participles (a passive infinitive); 'it' means the whistling.

sentences.context: Remembering what he had been engaged upon, he reached down to the floor
sentences.simple: He remembered what he had been working on. He reached down to the floor for his verses, looked hard at them for a minute, and then looked round for the Mole, to ask him if he knew a good rhyme for something or other.
sentences.grammar: 'Remembering ...' is a participle phrase with the same subject as the main clause ('he'); 'what he had been engaged upon' is a noun clause with the preposition at the end.

sentences.context: never mind what done it,” said the Mole, forgetting his grammar
sentences.simple: 'Well, never mind what did it,' said the Mole. He forgot his grammar because of the pain.
sentences.grammar: 'what done it' is wrong in standard English, which says 'what did it'; the book itself says the Mole forgets his grammar because of pain.

sentences.context: which was intelligent of Mole, because that was exactly what it was
sentences.simple: It seemed, as the Mole said to the Rat, like someone walking in carpet slippers that were too big for him and worn down at the heel. This was clever of the Mole, because that was just what it was.
sentences.grammar: 'which' begins a relative clause that talks about the whole remark before it (the Mole's guess), not about one noun.

sentences.context: they ought to have done so-and-so, or ought not to have done something else
sentences.simple: As he did not go into Society himself, he had an idea that these things did not really matter. He sat in his armchair at the head of the table and nodded in a serious way now and then as the animals told their story. He did not seem surprised or shocked at anything. He never said, 'I told you so,' or 'Just what I always said,' or that they should have done this, or should not have done something else.
sentences.grammar: 'ought to have + past participle' says what was the right thing to do in the past; 'ought not to have' says what was the wrong thing.

sentences.context: walks where he likes in this country, or I’ll know the reason why
sentences.simple: Any friend of mine may walk wherever he likes in this country. If he cannot, I will find out why.
sentences.grammar: 'X, or I'll know the reason why' uses 'or' to mean 'if not'; it is a warning that the Badger will find out why if his friend is stopped.

sentences.context: The Mole was staggered at the size, the extent, the ramifications of it all
sentences.simple: The Mole was amazed at the size of it all, how far it went, and how many branches it had. He was amazed at the length of the dim passages, the solid arched roofs of the crowded store-rooms, and the stonework everywhere, the pillars, the arches and the paved floors.
sentences.grammar: 'was staggered at' is followed by three nouns in a list ('the size, the extent, the ramifications'), each beginning with 'the'; a second list of 'the' nouns follows after the semicolon.

sentences.context: We others, who have long lost the more subtle of the physical senses
sentences.simple: We others, who lost the finer physical senses long ago, do not even have the right words for how an animal talks with the things around it, living or not. We have only the word 'smell', for example, for the whole range of fine feelings that murmur in the animal's nose night and day, calling, warning, urging on and pushing away.
sentences.grammar: 'who have long lost ...' is a relative clause inside the subject; 'have ... lost' is the present perfect, and the main verb 'have' comes much later in the sentence.

sentences.context: Since his escape on that bright morning he had hardly given it a thought
sentences.simple: Since he got away on that bright morning he had hardly thought about it. He had been so full of his new life, with all its pleasures, its surprises and its fresh and exciting experiences.
sentences.grammar: 'had hardly given it a thought' is past perfect with 'hardly'; 'so absorbed had he been' that follows puts 'had he been' after 'so absorbed' (inversion) for a strong effect.

sentences.context: and he had lost what he could hardly be said to have found
sentences.simple: He had lost something that he could hardly say he had found.
sentences.grammar: 'could hardly be said to have found' is a passive structure ('be said to') plus 'to have found' (perfect infinitive); 'what' means 'the thing that'.

sentences.context: It did not take long to prepare the brew and thrust the tin heater
sentences.simple: It did not take long to make the drink and push the tin heater into the red middle of the fire. Soon every field-mouse was sipping and coughing and choking (for a little warm spiced ale goes a long way). They wiped their eyes and laughed, and forgot that they had ever been cold in all their lives.
sentences.grammar: 'It did not take long to + verb' is a common pattern; 'a little mulled ale goes a long way' in the brackets is a saying meaning a small amount is strong.

sentences.context: in just the frame of mind that the tactful Rat had quietly worked
sentences.simple: He was now in just the mood that the Rat, who was careful of his feelings, had quietly worked to bring about in him.
sentences.grammar: 'that the tactful Rat had quietly worked to bring about' is a relative clause with 'that' as its object; 'bring about' is a phrasal verb meaning 'cause'.

sentences.context: which transform him from a (comparatively) good-looking Toad into an Object
sentences.simple: Those clothes change Toad from a fairly good-looking Toad into an Object. When a decent animal sees that Object, it becomes very angry.
sentences.grammar: 'which transform him from ... into ...' is a relative clause; the second 'which' ('which throws ... into a violent fit') describes the Object; the brackets give a small side remark.

sentences.context: Since you won’t yield to persuasion, we’ll try what force can do
sentences.simple: Since you will not give way when we try to persuade you, we will try what force can do.
sentences.grammar: 'Since' here means 'because'; 'what force can do' is a noun clause that is the object of 'try'; 'yield to' means 'give way to'.

sentences.context: the only difficulty that presents itself in this otherwise very clear case is
sentences.simple: 'In my view,' said the Chairman of the Bench of Magistrates cheerfully, 'the only difficulty in this case, which is otherwise very clear, is how we can possibly make the punishment hard enough for the rogue who never changes and the hardened ruffian that we see shaking with fear in the dock before us.'
sentences.grammar: 'the only difficulty ... is, how we can ...' puts a long subject before 'is'; the noun clause 'how we can possibly make it ...' says what the difficulty is.

sentences.context: should aught untoward befall, thy old head shall answer for his
sentences.simple: Guard him with all your skill. And remember well, greybeard, if anything bad should happen, your old head will pay for his, and a curse on both of them!
sentences.grammar: 'should aught untoward befall' means 'if anything bad should happen'; it starts with 'should' (inversion) instead of 'if'; 'thy' is an old word for 'your'.

sentences.context: Though it was past ten o’clock at night, the sky still clung to
sentences.simple: It was past ten o'clock at night, but the sky still held some last light from the day that had gone. The heavy heat of the very hot afternoon broke up and rolled away at the cool touch of the short midsummer night.
sentences.grammar: 'Though ...' starts a clause of contrast; the main clause with 'clung to and retained' has two verbs sharing one object ('skirts of light'); after the semicolon a second main clause tells what the heat did.

sentences.context: Since it was to end so soon, I almost wish I had never
sentences.simple: Since it was going to end so soon, I almost wish I had never heard it.
sentences.grammar: 'Since' means 'because'; 'was to end' is a future in the past; 'I wish I had never heard' is the past perfect after 'wish' and talks about something that cannot be changed.

sentences.context: He might not refuse, were Death himself waiting to strike him instantly
sentences.simple: He could not refuse, even if Death himself were waiting to strike him at once, after he had looked with human eyes on things that should stay hidden.
sentences.grammar: 'were Death himself waiting' means 'even if Death were waiting'; the verb 'were' is put first (inversion) instead of 'if'; 'might not' here means 'was not able to'.

sentences.context: As one wakened suddenly from a beautiful dream, who struggles to recall it
sentences.simple: Think of a person who is woken suddenly from a beautiful dream and tries hard to remember it. He can keep only a dim feeling of how beautiful it was, until that too fades away, and he sadly accepts the hard, cold waking and all it costs him. So Mole, after struggling with his memory for a short time, shook his head sadly and followed the Rat.
sentences.grammar: This is a long comparison: 'As one ... so Mole ...'; the 'who' clause adds more about the person, 'Till that, too, fades away' starts a new part, and 'so Mole' finally says who is like him.

sentences.context: Lest the awful remembrance should remain and grow, and overshadow mirth and pleasure
sentences.simple: It is given so that the awful memory should not stay and grow and cast a shadow on happiness and fun. It is also given so that the great memory that would not leave them should not spoil all the later lives of little animals who have been helped out of trouble. In this way they can be happy and light-hearted as before.
sentences.grammar: 'Lest ... should ...' means 'so that ... will not'; it is an old, formal way to say what must be avoided.

sentences.context: How can I hope to be ever set at large again” (he said)
sentences.simple: How can I hope ever to be free again, I who have been put in prison so fairly for stealing such a handsome motorcar in such a bold way, and for such wild and clever cheek to so many fat, red-faced policemen?
sentences.grammar: 'set at large' means 'set free'; '(he said)' is put in the middle of Toad's speech; 'who have been imprisoned' is a relative clause that explains why he has no hope.

sentences.context: She was particularly fond of animals, and, besides her canary
sentences.simple: She was very fond of animals. Besides her canary, whose cage hung on a nail in the thick wall of the tower by day, to the great annoyance of prisoners who liked an after-dinner sleep, and was covered with a cloth on the parlour table at night, she kept several black-and-white mice and a restless squirrel in a wheel.
sentences.grammar: This is a long sentence: 'besides her canary' starts a side phrase, and 'whose cage hung ... and was shrouded ...' is a relative clause with two verbs; the main clause comes late ('she kept ...').

sentences.context: At last —somehow —he never rightly understood how —he burst the barriers
sentences.simple: At last, somehow (he never really understood how), he broke through the barriers, reached the goal and arrived at the place where all waistcoat pockets always are. There he found not only no money, but no pocket to hold it, and no waistcoat to hold the pocket!
sentences.grammar: The dashes put a side remark ('he never rightly understood how') in the middle; 'not only no money, but no pocket ..., and no waistcoat ...' is a list that gets smaller each time.

sentences.context: I could be sworn that I heard another following us
sentences.simple: It is very strange. We are the last train running in this direction tonight, and yet I could swear that I heard another following us!
sentences.grammar: 'could be sworn' is an old passive form meaning 'I could swear'; 'heard another following us' uses 'heard + object + -ing'.

sentences.context: By this not very convincing artifice, she explained, aided by picturesque fiction
sentences.simple: She explained that by this trick, which was not very convincing, with the help of a colourful story that she could make up herself, she hoped to keep her job, in spite of how suspicious things looked.
sentences.grammar: 'she explained' is a side remark; 'aided by ...' is a participle phrase that says what helped; 'in spite of' at the end gives the opposite.

sentences.context: Rat, ever observant of all winged movement, saw that it was
sentences.simple: The Rat, who always watched anything that flew, saw that the flying was going more towards the south each day.
sentences.grammar: 'ever observant of ...' is a phrase that describes Rat and is put between commas; 'it was taking daily a southing tendency' has an old word order, with 'daily' between the verb and its object.

sentences.context: One gets unsettled, depressed, and inclined to be querulous
sentences.simple: One becomes unsettled, sad and likely to complain.
sentences.grammar: 'One' means 'a person in general'; 'inclined to be ...' means 'likely to be ...'; the three words that follow 'gets' are joined in a list.

sentences.context: and the fortunes and adventures they had gone to seek or found unseeking
sentences.simple: There, half-hidden in the thick, cool tangle under the hedge, he could think about the hard road and all the wonderful world that it led to. He could think about all the travellers who might have walked on it, and the good luck and adventures that they had gone to look for, or had found without looking.
sentences.grammar: 'they had gone to seek or found unseeking' joins two verbs with 'or'; 'unseeking' means 'not looking for it'; 'had gone' and 'found' share the subject 'they'.

sentences.context: Take the adventure, heed the call, now ere the irrevocable moment passes
sentences.simple: Take the adventure, listen to the call, now before the moment that cannot be taken back goes by!
sentences.grammar: 'Take ..., heed ...' are commands; 'ere' is an old word meaning 'before'; the order of words is old and poetic.

sentences.context: He would probably have been aroused much earlier, had he not slept
sentences.simple: He would probably have woken much earlier if he had not slept for some weeks on straw over stone floors. He had almost forgotten how nice thick blankets feel when they are pulled up round the chin.
sentences.grammar: 'had he not slept' means 'if he had not slept' (inversion); 'would probably have been aroused' is the third conditional in the passive and talks about the past that did not happen.

sentences.context: It is all very well, when you have a light heart, and a
sentences.simple: It is all very well to follow where the road calls and points, without caring where it goes, when you have a light heart, a clear conscience, money in your pocket, and nobody searching the country to drag you off to prison again.
sentences.grammar: 'It is all very well to follow ...' means 'it is fine to follow ...' (but there is a problem); the long 'when you have ...' list comes between 'well' and 'to follow'.

sentences.context: Alas! they should have thought, they ought to have been more prudent
sentences.simple: Alas! They should have thought. They should have been more careful. They should have remembered to stop the motorcar before playing any such tricks.
sentences.grammar: 'should have + past participle' and 'ought to have been' both say what was the right thing to do but did not happen; the three clauses repeat the same idea.

sentences.context: Who was it got them to give him a lift?
sentences.simple: Who was it that got them to give him a ride?
sentences.grammar: 'Who was it got ...' is a spoken form of 'Who was it that got ...'; 'got them to give' is 'get + person + to + verb', meaning to persuade someone.

sentences.context: Humbugged everybody —made ’em all do exactly what I wanted
sentences.simple: I tricked everybody and made them all do exactly what I wanted.
sentences.grammar: This is a list of short sentences without 'I'; 'humbugged' is a verb made from the noun 'humbug' (a person who pretends); '’em' is a spoken short form of 'them'.

sentences.context: But if you will be mixed up with them —as you generally are
sentences.simple: But if you insist on being mixed up with motorcars, as you usually are five minutes after you have started, why steal them?
sentences.grammar: 'if you will be' with a stressed 'will' means 'if you insist on being'; 'as you generally are' is a side comment between dashes.

sentences.context: Now I come to the most painful and tragic part of my story
sentences.simple: Now I come to the most painful and sad part of my story.
sentences.grammar: 'the most painful and tragic part' uses 'the most + adjective' for the superlative of long adjectives, joined with 'and'.

sentences.context: They argued from history,” continued the Rat. “They said that no criminal laws
sentences.simple: 'They argued from the past,' the Rat went on. 'They said that no criminal laws had ever been known to win against cheek and good talk like yours, together with the power of a full purse.'
sentences.grammar: 'had ever been known to prevail' is the passive past perfect with 'to + verb'; 'such as yours, combined with ...' joins two things that work together.

sentences.context: There are more ways of getting back a place than taking it by storm
sentences.simple: There are other ways to get a place back, besides taking it by force.
sentences.grammar: 'more ways of getting back ... than taking ...' compares two '-ing' forms with 'more ... than'; 'by storm' means 'by a strong attack'.

sentences.context: The Toad was so anxious not to be left out that he took
sentences.simple: Toad was so worried about being left out that he took the lower place they gave him without a word, and the animals set off.
sentences.grammar: 'so anxious not to be left out that he took up ...' is a 'so ... that' result clause; 'assigned to him' is a past participle phrase telling which position; 'without a murmur' means 'without complaining'.

sentences.context: Well might the terrified weasels dive under the tables and spring madly
sentences.simple: It was no surprise that the frightened weasels dived under the tables and sprang wildly up at the windows.
sentences.grammar: 'Well might + subject + verb' is an old way to put the helper verb first; it means 'it is easy to understand why' they did this.

sentences.context: Through the broken windows the shrieks of terrified weasels escaping across the lawn
sentences.simple: Through the broken windows came the faint sound of the screams of frightened weasels running away across the lawn. On the floor lay about a dozen of the enemy, and the Mole was busy putting handcuffs on them.
sentences.grammar: This is a sentence with the order changed: the place 'Through the broken windows' comes first, and the subject 'the shrieks' comes before 'were borne'; 'on whom the Mole was busily engaged in fitting handcuffs' is a relative clause; 'engaged in + -ing' means 'busy doing'.

sentences.context: Toad, after due consultation with his friends, selected a handsome gold chain
sentences.simple: After talking it over properly with his friends, Toad chose a fine gold chain and a locket set with pearls, and sent them to the gaoler's daughter with a letter. Even the Badger agreed that the letter was modest, thankful and full of praise.
sentences.grammar: 'after due consultation with his friends' is a phrase placed between commas; 'which he dispatched' is a relative clause; 'a letter that even the Badger admitted to be ...' has 'admitted to be' + adjectives.

head over ears.example: head over ears in deep water
